short: the most client connections a server accepts at once. 100 by default, each one a backend process; a few slots are kept for superusers.
a small set of open server connections lent out to many clients, so the server runs near the work it can do at once and the rest wait cheaply.
a pool mode that gives a client a server connection for one transaction only. scales well, and loses session state such as SET, SQL PREPARE and session advisory locks.
one query for a list, then one more per row for a relation, usually from lazy loading in an ORM. each is fast; the round trips add up.
fetching a relation up front for every row, with a join or one WHERE id = ANY($1) query, instead of once per row on first access.
one table name over several real tables, split by a partition key into ranges, lists of values or hash buckets.
skipping partitions that can't match the WHERE on the partition key: while planning, at executor start (Subplans Removed) or while running (never executed).
the partition that takes rows no other partition accepts. it has to be checked whenever a new partition is added.
a standby that answers read-only queries. always a little behind the primary.
how far a standby is behind the primary, in bytes of WAL or in time. pg_stat_replication shows write, flush and replay lag.
a client always sees its own earlier writes. with replicas: route to the primary after a write, or wait until the replica has replayed the write's LSN.
the column that decides which shard (machine) a row lives on. queries that include it go to one shard; the rest go to all.
a shard that gets far more load than the others, from a busy key or a key like time that sends every new write to one place.
during a network partition, a replicated register can't be both linearizable and available. conjectured by Brewer, proved by Gilbert and Lynch.
Abadi's extension of CAP: if partitioned, availability or consistency; else, latency or consistency.
each operation appears to take effect at one instant between its call and its return, so a finished write is seen by every later read.
operations that could have influenced each other are seen in that order everywhere; unrelated ones may appear in any order.
if writes stop, every copy eventually returns the same value. nothing is promised about reads in the meantime.
serializable transactions in an order that respects real time: serializability plus linearizability.
atomic commit across databases: every participant prepares and votes, then all commit or all roll back. blocks if the coordinator dies after the votes.
a transaction after PREPARE TRANSACTION: durable, detached from its session, holding its locks until COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED. survives restarts.
a consensus algorithm: a leader per term, a replicated log, and a majority to elect or commit anything. by Ongaro and Ousterhout.
a set of replicas large enough that any two overlap. with n replicas, w + r > n makes every read meet the latest write.
spanner's clock API: an interval guaranteed to contain the real time. commits wait out its width so timestamps follow real-time order.
storage moved out of the database server into a replicated service that compute nodes share, as in aurora and neon.
